steps.observation: Work on this for 60 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here are the key differences between DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid):

1. Sugar backbone  
   • DNA contains deoxyribose (lacks an –OH group on its 2′ carbon).  
   • RNA contains ribose (has an –OH group on its 2′ carbon).  

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA’s four bases are adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T).  
   • RNA’s four bases are A, G, C and uracil (U) instead of thymine.  

3. Strand structure  
   • DNA is typically double-stranded, forming a stable double helix.  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded and can fold into complex 3D shapes.  

4. Stability  
   • DNA’s deoxyribose and lack of 2′-OH make it chemically more stable—ideal for long-term storage of genetic information.  
   • RNA’s 2′-OH makes it more reactive and less stable, suited for short-term tasks.  

5. Location in the cell  
   • DNA resides mainly in the nucleus (and in mitochondria/chloroplasts).  
   • RNA is synthesized in the nucleus but functions throughout the cytoplasm; different types may localize to specific organelles.  

6. Primary functions  
   • DNA stores and transmits hereditary information.  
   • RNA translates that information into proteins (mRNA), catalyzes reactions (rRNA), transports amino acids (tRNA), and regulates gene expression (microRNA, siRNA, etc.).  

7. Lifespan and turnover  
   • DNA is long-lived and replicated only during cell division.  
   • RNA molecules have varying lifespans—from minutes (some mRNAs) to days (some rRNAs)—and are constantly synthesized and degraded.  

In summary, DNA is a stable, double-stranded repository of genetic information; RNA is a versatile, generally single-stranded molecule that reads, carries, folds, regulates, and sometimes even catalyzes biochemical processes.
